MASH. A sitcom that aired on CBS from nineteen seventy-two to nineteen eighty-three, following a unit of American surgeons and support staff at a Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War. Balancing dark humor, antiwar sentiment, and genuine pathos, the show proved that sitcoms could address the absurdity and tragedy of military conflict while building ensemble camaraderie and character depth.

Alan Alda starred as Captain Benjamin "Hawkeye" Pierce, the show's conscience and comedic heart—a surgeon using humor to cope with wartime trauma. The Mobile Army Surgical Hospital was a real U.S. military unit that served during the Korean War from nineteen fifty to nineteen fifty-three. Over its eleven-season run, the show shifted from broad comedy in early seasons to increasingly dramatic storytelling, blending sitcom tropes with genuine emotional weight.

The antiwar message grew stronger as the Vietnam War dragged on in reality; the show became a cultural mirror of American ambivalence about military intervention. Its final episode, "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen" in nineteen eighty-three, drew one hundred six million viewers—one of the largest television audiences in history. Alan Alda won four Emmy Awards and became the show's creative force as director and writer. MASH introduced the dramedy format, proving sitcoms could hold both laughs and tears simultaneously.
